alignment.note: Greek κατά + accusative expresses distributive/temporal sense ('at [the time of]'); Latin renders Per diem ('throughout the day'); Syriac ܒܟܠ ('on every') makes the iterative force explicit, agreeing in distributive sense though using a different preposition base.
δέ / ܕܝܢ / autem — the postpositive adversative particle is attested identically in all three traditions.
ἑορτήν / ܥܐܕܐ / diem festum — 'feast'; the parenthetical transliteration (he'ortēn) is a gloss of the same lexeme and aligns with the single Syriac feast-noun and the Latin two-word phrase.

Greek expresses customary action with a single imperfect ἀπέλυεν ('he was releasing'); Latin periphrasis solebat dimittere ('was accustomed to release') makes the habitual aspect explicit; Syriac achieves the same with the customary particle ܡܥܕ + auxiliary ܗܘܐ plus the infinitive ܠܡܫܪܐ, a triple-token customary periphrasis.

Greek uses the simple accusative noun δέσμιον ('a prisoner'); Latin recasts this as a partitive prepositional phrase ex vinctis ('from among the bound ones'); Syriac ܐܣܝܪܐ retains the simple participial noun 'prisoner', so Greek and Syriac agree against the Latin partitive construction.

The relative ὃν ('whom') in Greek is matched by Syriac ܐܝܢܐ ('whichever one') and Latin's intensifying quemcumque ('whomsoever'); Latin and Syriac both heighten the indefinite force of the simple Greek relative, reflecting the popular-choice nuance of the custom.

Greek παρῃτοῦντο (imperfect of παραιτέομαι, 'they kept requesting/begging off') is rendered in Syriac by ܫܐܠܝܢ (root sh-a-l, 'they ask'), the standard verb for petition; Latin petissent (pluperfect subjunctive 'they had asked') aligns lexically but shifts to subjunctive mood within the relative clause, a syntactic rather than lexical divergence.
